subject: English
learning_objectives: Read and recite the poem 'Vocation' by Rabindranath Tagore with correct rhythm and expression
Identify the three workers the child meets — hawker, gardener, and watchman — and explain why the child envies each
Understand the central theme: a child's longing for freedom from rules and restrictions
Appreciate the literary device of contrast between the child's restricted life and the workers' apparent freedom
Identify poetic devices used in the poem: imagery, simile, repetition, and onomatopoeia
Understand the meaning of the word 'vocation' and its significance as the poem's title
Connect the poem's theme of childhood freedom to real-life experiences
Answer comprehension and MCQ questions accurately based on the poem
prerequisite_knowledge: Basic understanding of what a poem is — stanzas, rhyme, rhythm
Familiarity with the concept of a 'job' or 'occupation' (the meaning of vocation)
Knowledge of common workers seen in Indian streets: hawkers, gardeners, watchmen
Ability to identify the speaker's voice in a poem

introduction.why_important: This poem captures a feeling every child knows — the wish to be free, to do what you want without being told to stop. By reading it, students learn how to express such universal emotions through poetry, and how to look at the world around them with a poet's eye.
introduction.real_life_relevance: Every student has felt restricted at some point — forced to go to bed early, scolded for getting muddy, told to come inside. Tagore's poem puts those exact feelings into beautiful words, reminding students that their emotions are universal and worthy of expression.
introduction.karnataka_context: Rabindranath Tagore, though born in Bengal, is one of the most celebrated literary figures across all of India, including Karnataka. His works have been translated into Kannada, and Tagore Jayanti is celebrated in Karnataka schools every year on 7 May. The scenes in the poem — a hawker crying wares on the road, a mali (gardener) digging in the soil, a watchman with his lantern at night — are deeply familiar sights in Karnataka towns and villages, from the bangle sellers of Chickpet in Bengaluru to the night watchmen of old Mysuru neighbourhoods.
introduction.connection_to_previous_learning: This poem connects to the themes of freedom and cleverness explored in Chapter 10 (A Strange Wrestling Match), where Vijay Singh longed to break free of his boast's constraints. Here too, the child longs to break free — but from the gentler constraints of school and bedtime rules.

poem_text.stanza_1: When the gong sounds ten in the morning and I walk to school by the road, / I see the hawker crying, 'Bangles, crystal bangles!' / There is nothing to hurry him on, there is no road he must take, / no place he must go to, no time when he must come home. / I wish I were a hawker, spending my day on the road, / calling out, 'Bangles, crystal bangles!'
poem_text.stanza_2: When school is over and it is afternoon, / I am home with my lessons to learn. / But I watch through the window a gardener digging the ground. / He does what he likes with his spade, / he soils his clothes with dust, / nobody takes him to task if he gets baked in the sun or gets wet. / I wish I were a gardener digging away at the garden / with nobody to stop me from digging.
poem_text.stanza_3: Just as it gets dark in the evening and my mother sends me to bed, / I can see through my open window the watchman walking up and down. / The lane is dark and lonely, and the street-lamp stands like a giant / with one red eye in its head. / The watchman swings his lantern and walks with his shadow at his side, / and never once goes to bed in his life. / I wish I were a watchman walking the street all night, / chasing the shadows with my lantern.

characters.name: The Child (Speaker)
characters.role: A school-going boy who observes three workers at three different times of day and envies their apparent freedom from rules and routine

characters.name: The Hawker
characters.role: A bangle seller the child sees in the morning on his way to school — free to walk any road, go anywhere, and cry out his wares without a fixed schedule

characters.name: The Gardener
characters.role: A man digging in the garden in the afternoon — free to soil his clothes, work in sun or rain, with no one to scold or restrict him

characters.name: The Watchman
characters.role: A night guard walking the dark lane with a lantern — free to stay awake all night, walk in the darkness, and chase shadows, while the child must sleep

plot: The poem is told from the perspective of a school-going child at three times of day: morning, afternoon, and evening.
In the morning (when the gong sounds ten), the child walks to school and sees a hawker selling bangles. The hawker has no fixed road or time — he is free. The child wishes he were a hawker.

In the afternoon, the child returns from school and must sit with lessons. He sees a gardener digging outside his window — working freely in sun and mud, scolded by no one. The child wishes he were a gardener.

In the evening, the mother sends the child to bed. Through the window, he watches the watchman walking up and down the dark lane with a lantern. The watchman never goes to bed. The child wishes he were a watchman.
Each stanza ends with the child's wish — a refrain that builds the poem's emotional rhythm and central theme: the longing for freedom from childhood restrictions.
story_summary.moral: Children naturally long for freedom and find rules and routines restrictive. However, they do not fully see the hardships behind the apparent freedom of working people. The poem gently reminds us that what looks like freedom from the outside may carry its own burdens — and that childhood, with all its rules, is also a time of wonder and imagination.

core_concepts.concept_name: Vocation and the Longing for Freedom
core_concepts.simple_explanation: A vocation is a job or calling. The child in the poem sees three workers and wishes he had their job — not because the jobs are great, but because they seem free from rules.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: The word 'vocation' comes from the Latin word 'vocare', meaning 'to call' — it means a job or profession that feels like a calling. In this poem, Tagore uses the word cleverly: the child is 'called' to envy three vocations — hawker, gardener, and watchman — not because they are glamorous but because they seem to offer freedom. The child is bound by the clock (school at ten), by homework (lessons after school), and by bedtime (mother's orders at night). Each worker he sees operates outside these restrictions. The hawker has no fixed time or path, the gardener has no dress code or supervisor, and the watchman never sleeps. The child interprets this as complete freedom. This is the poem's central irony — the child does not see the hard work, weather, loneliness, or exhaustion these workers endure. His envy is based on imagination, not reality.
core_concepts.real_life_example: A student sitting inside doing homework on a rainy afternoon watches a construction worker outside, unconcerned about the rain, working freely. The student thinks, 'How lucky — no homework!' But the worker is tired, wet, and earning barely enough. The child's view is incomplete — just like the speaker in the poem.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: In Bengaluru's traditional markets like Chickpet and KR Market, one can still see bangle sellers and street hawkers calling out their wares daily, much like the hawker in the poem. Karnataka's Janapada songs are full of workers — kadu goots (forest workers), potters, weavers — celebrated in folk poetry as free, rooted people. Tagore's hawker echoes this tradition of honouring the working person's spirit.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students often think the poem is simply saying that the hawker's, gardener's, and watchman's lives are better than the child's. The poem is actually more nuanced — it shows the child's innocent, incomplete perception of freedom. The poem does not endorse giving up school; it celebrates childhood imagination and the universal longing to be unrestricted.
core_concepts.memory_tip: Remember the three workers with THREE F's: Hawker = Free to roam, Gardener = Free to dig, Watchman = Free to stay awake. The child wants all three freedoms — but has none!

core_concepts.concept_name: Structure of the Poem — Three Times of Day
core_concepts.simple_explanation: The poem is organised into three stanzas, each set at a different time of day — morning, afternoon, and evening. This structure mirrors the child's full day of restrictions.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Tagore structures the poem around the cycle of a child's day — from the morning walk to school (10 o'clock), through the afternoon of homework, to the enforced bedtime at evening. Each time period brings a new restriction and a new worker who seems exempt from it. This structure is deeply intentional: it shows that the child's sense of being restricted is not limited to one moment — it runs through the entire day. The three-part structure also creates a rhythm that mirrors the poem's emotional build-up. Each stanza follows the same pattern: (a) what the child must do, (b) what the worker does freely, (c) the child's wish. This repetition is itself a poetic device — it reinforces the child's persistent longing.
core_concepts.real_life_example: Think of your own school day: you have a fixed wake-up time, fixed school hours, fixed homework time, and fixed bedtime. Now think of three people you see at different points of the day who seem free — perhaps a shopkeeper, a chai stall owner, someone playing cricket. The poem maps this exact pattern.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Karnataka's traditional folk poetry, especially Vachana literature by saints like Basavanna, often structured verses in repeating patterns that built emotional intensity — similar to Tagore's three-stanza structure. The concept of 'anubhava mantapa' (a hall of experience) in Basavanna's tradition was about giving voice to all people's experiences, including workers — exactly what Tagore does in this poem.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students sometimes treat the three stanzas as three separate poems. They are one continuous poem with a deliberate structure. The stanzas are connected by the common speaker (the child) and the common theme (longing for freedom). The time progression — morning → afternoon → evening — is a single narrative arc, not three unrelated scenes.
core_concepts.memory_tip: MAE: Morning = Hawker, Afternoon = Gardener, Evening = Watchman. MAE stands for the child's day of restrictions. Also read: 'My Awful Enclosure' — the child feels enclosed all day!

core_concepts.simple_explanation: Tagore uses special language tools — imagery, simile, repetition, and onomatopoeia — to make the poem vivid and musical. These are called poetic devices.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Several literary devices make 'Vocation' memorable. Imagery: Tagore creates visual pictures — the hawker crying on the road, the gardener soiling his clothes, the watchman walking with his shadow. These images bring the poem to life. Simile: 'the street-lamp stands like a giant with one red eye in its head' — comparing the street lamp to a one-eyed giant is a memorable and slightly eerie image that captures a child's nighttime imagination. Repetition: The phrase 'I wish I were...' repeats in each stanza, reinforcing the child's constant longing. Onomatopoeia: Words like 'crying' (the hawker's call) and 'swings' (the lantern) carry the sound of the action. Personification: The shadow walks 'at his side' like a companion. Together, these devices make a simple childhood emotion feel rich, musical, and universal.
core_concepts.real_life_example: When you say 'the thunder clapped' or 'the fire danced', you are using personification and imagery — the same tools Tagore uses. Next time you describe something, try giving it a human quality or comparing it to something unexpected. That is how poets like Tagore make ordinary scenes extraordinary.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Kannada poetry, especially from the Vachana tradition and later the Navodaya movement (with poets like Kuvempu and D.R. Bendre), is rich in nature imagery and personification — much like Tagore's simile of the street lamp as a giant. Kuvempu's famous poem 'O Nanna Chaitanya' uses imagery of nature to express childhood wonder, closely paralleling Tagore's use of sensory images in 'Vocation'.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students often miss the simile of the street-lamp-as-giant because it appears in the middle of a stanza rather than standing alone. Also, students sometimes call 'Bangles, crystal bangles!' alliteration — it is actually the hawker's cry (direct speech) and an example of onomatopoeia/imagery, not strict alliteration. Read carefully before labelling devices.
core_concepts.memory_tip: Remember the four devices with SIRP: Simile (lamp like a giant), Imagery (hawker on the road), Repetition ('I wish I were'), Personification (shadow at his side). SIRP — Tagore's poem is STIRRING because of SIRP!

key_terms_glossary.meaning: A job, profession, or occupation — especially one that feels like a natural calling. The poem's title refers to the three jobs (hawker, gardener, watchman) that the child wishes to have, drawn to them not for the work itself but for the freedom they seem to offer.

A street vendor or peddler who travels from place to place selling goods, often calling out loudly to attract buyers. In the poem, the hawker sells bangles and has no fixed route or time — he roams freely.
A large metal disc that makes a deep ringing sound when struck. 'When the gong sounds ten' means when the clock strikes ten o'clock in the morning — the time the child must leave for school.
Glass or crystal bracelets worn as jewellery, commonly sold by street hawkers in India. The hawker in the poem cries 'Bangles, crystal bangles!' to attract customers as he walks the roads.
A garden tool with a flat, sharp blade used for digging soil. The gardener in the poem uses a spade to dig the garden freely, soiling his clothes without any scolding.
Scolds, reprimands, or criticises someone for a mistake or behaviour. The poem says 'nobody takes him to task' — meaning nobody scolds the gardener for getting dirty or wet.
To be exposed to the hot sun for a long time, becoming very hot or uncomfortable. The gardener can work under the burning sun without anyone stopping or scolding him.
A portable light source with a handle, used before modern electric torches. The watchman in the poem carries a lantern as he walks the dark street at night, swinging it as he goes.

Descriptive language that creates a vivid mental picture or appeals to the senses. Tagore's poem is full of imagery — the bangle seller's cry, the dark lane, the swinging lantern — that helps readers see and feel the scene.

A figure of speech that compares two different things using 'like' or 'as'. In the poem, 'the street-lamp stands like a giant with one red eye in its head' is a simile comparing the street lamp to a one-eyed giant.

worked_examples.question: Why does the child in the poem envy the hawker? What does the child wish and why?
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: Identify the setting — The child is walking to school at 10 in the morning when he sees the hawker.

Step 2: Describe the hawker's life as the child sees it — The hawker has no fixed road, no fixed time, and no place he must go. He is free to walk anywhere, cry his wares, and return whenever he likes.
Step 3: Contrast with the child's life — The child must walk a fixed road to school at a fixed time. He has no such freedom of movement.
Step 4: State the child's wish — The child wishes he were a hawker, spending his day on the road, calling out 'Bangles, crystal bangles!' — free and unrestricted.
Step 5: Explain the deeper reason — The child envies not the work of selling bangles, but the freedom from routine, fixed paths, and mandatory destinations.
Conclusion: The child's envy is rooted in his longing for freedom from the rules that govern his school day. The hawker represents the opposite of a structured, supervised life.

worked_examples.question: Use the phrase 'takes him to task' in a sentence connected to the poem 'Vocation'.
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: Recall meaning — 'Takes him to task' means to scold or reprimand someone for their behaviour or actions.
Step 2: Connect to the poem — The gardener soils his clothes with dust, gets baked in the sun, and gets wet — but 'nobody takes him to task'. No one scolds him for any of this.

Step 3: Write sentence: 'The child envied the gardener because, unlike himself who would be scolded for getting muddy, nobody took the gardener to task even when he soiled his clothes digging in the sun.'

worked_examples.question: The child in the poem thinks the hawker, gardener, and watchman are completely free. Do you think this is true? What does the poem teach us about how children see the world?
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: State the child's view — The child believes the three workers are free — free from time, rules, dress codes, and sleep schedules.

Step 2: Examine the reality — The hawker walks long distances in all weather to sell bangles; the gardener does hard physical labour in the sun; the watchman stays awake all night in a dark, lonely lane. These are not easy lives.

Step 3: Identify the gap — The child sees only the apparent freedom, not the hardship. This is because children naturally focus on what they want (freedom from restrictions) rather than the full picture.
Step 4: Connect to the poem's moral — The poem gently shows that childhood imagination sees the world through the lens of desire. This is not wrong — it is a beautiful part of being a child.

Conclusion: The poem teaches us that children's perceptions are shaped by their immediate feelings and experiences. It also reminds adults to value childhood imagination, even when it is incomplete. The real lesson is empathy — learning to see others' lives more fully as we grow.

quick_check_questions.after_concept: Vocation and the Longing for Freedom

questions.q: Who are the three workers the child sees in the poem 'Vocation'?
questions.a: The three workers are: (1) a hawker (bangle seller), seen in the morning; (2) a gardener, seen in the afternoon; and (3) a watchman, seen in the evening.

questions.q: What does the hawker sell in the poem?
questions.a: The hawker sells bangles — specifically called 'crystal bangles' in the poem. He walks the roads crying 'Bangles, crystal bangles!' to attract buyers.

questions.q: Why does the child wish he were a gardener? What freedom does the gardener seem to have?
questions.a: The child wishes he were a gardener because the gardener can do what he likes with his spade, soil his clothes with dust, get baked in the sun or get wet — all without anyone scolding him. The child, in contrast, would be scolded for getting dirty or going out in the rain.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'never once goes to bed in his life' tell us about the watchman?
questions.a: The phrase tells us that the watchman stays up all night — he does not go to bed. The child, who is forced to sleep when it gets dark, envies this. From the child's perspective, the watchman has the ultimate freedom: never having to obey a bedtime.

questions.q: If you were to add a fourth stanza to this poem, which worker would you choose and what freedom would they represent? Explain.
questions.a: Answers will vary. Example: A student might choose a chai-walla (tea seller) seen during school lunch break — free to talk to everyone, with no tests or homework. The student could write: 'I wish I were a chai-walla, talking to people all day, / with no exam to worry about, no bell to obey.'

key_takeaways: The poem 'Vocation' is written by Rabindranath Tagore — Nobel Prize-winning Indian poet, author, and philosopher.
The speaker is a school-going child who observes a hawker, a gardener, and a watchman at three times of day.
The hawker is seen in the morning — he has no fixed path, time, or destination; the child wishes to be him.
The gardener is seen in the afternoon — he can work freely, get dirty, and is scolded by no one; the child wishes to be him.
The watchman is seen in the evening — he walks the dark street all night with a lantern and never sleeps; the child wishes to be him.
The central theme is a child's longing for freedom from rules, fixed routines, and restrictions.
The poem uses: Simile ('lamp like a giant'), Imagery (hawker on the road, dark lane), Repetition ('I wish I were'), and Personification (shadow walking at his side).
The poem's title 'Vocation' is ironic — it refers to the jobs the child envies, not the child's own calling.
The child's perception is innocent and incomplete — the workers' lives are actually hard, not free.
Karnataka connection: Tagore Jayanti is celebrated in Karnataka schools; the scenes in the poem mirror everyday sights in Karnataka towns and cities.

revision_notes: The poem 'Vocation' is written by Rabindranath Tagore, India's first Nobel Prize winner in Literature (1913). It is a three-stanza poem told by a school-going child who observes three workers across his day. In the morning, walking to school when the gong sounds ten, he sees a hawker selling crystal bangles — free to walk any road with no fixed time. In the afternoon, forced to sit with lessons, he watches a gardener digging freely in sun and mud, scolded by nobody. In the evening, sent to bed by his mother, he sees a watchman walking the dark lane with a lantern, never sleeping. Each stanza ends with 'I wish I were...' — the refrain that carries the poem's central emotion: a child's longing for freedom from rules and routine. The word 'vocation' means a job or calling. The irony is that the child envies these vocations not for their work but for their apparent freedom. Key poetic devices: Simile ('the street-lamp stands like a giant with one red eye'), Imagery (crystal bangles, dark lane, swinging lantern), Repetition ('I wish I were'), Personification (shadow walking at his side). Key vocabulary: gong, hawker, crystal bangles, spade, takes him to task, baked in the sun, lantern. The poem's moral: children see the world through their own desires; what looks like freedom from outside often carries hidden hardship.
must_remember_facts: Poet: Rabindranath Tagore — Nobel Prize in Literature, 1913; first Asian to win the Nobel Prize.
The poem has three stanzas corresponding to three times of day: morning, afternoon, and evening.
Morning: Hawker selling 'crystal bangles' — no fixed road, no fixed time.
Afternoon: Gardener digging with a spade — can get dirty, no one scolds.
Evening: Watchman with lantern in dark lane — never goes to bed.
The child's refrain: 'I wish I were a hawker/gardener/watchman'.
Key simile: 'the street-lamp stands like a giant with one red eye in its head'.
Poetic devices: Simile, Imagery, Repetition, Personification.
Title meaning: 'Vocation' = a job or calling — the poem is about the vocations the child longs to have.
The poem's deeper truth: the child's view of freedom is incomplete — the workers' lives are actually hard.
